candidates.title: Vertex of y = −2(x + 3)^2 + 5 (h-sign)
candidates.student_facing: Look at y = −2(x + 3)^2 + 5. Name the vertex of this parabola.
candidates.source_stem:
For each quadratic relation, list the transformations you need to apply to y = x^2 to graph the relation. Then sketch the graph.

a) y = x^2 − 2

b) y = −4x^2 + 3

c) y = (1/2)(x − 1)^2 − 4

d) y = −2(x + 3)^2 + 5
candidates.answer_verification: Local Nelson bank item has no key. Focus on part (d) only; the full stem also asks for a transformation list (A2.5/A2.6, already taught).

provenance.licence: unknown (commercial textbook excerpt in local bank; licence not recorded in the bank file)

instructional_roles: names vertex (h, k) from the equation
candidates.reason: Closest existing bank item to the brief’s h-sign case f(x) = (x + 3)^2 + 1. Students who read the written plus as a right shift place the vertex at (3, 5) instead of (−3, 5). Isolating the vertex ask keeps this on A2.10 inspection, not a new transformation lesson.

candidates.title: Predict vertex of (x + 3)^2 + 1, then check sliders
candidates.student_facing: Before you move anything, name the vertex of f(x) = (x + 3)^2 + 1. Then set the sliders so the graph matches that equation and check.
candidates.source_stem: Change the parameters to investigate their effect on the function graph. Compare g(x) to f(x). Point A is the vertex of f(x) and B is the vertex of g(x).
candidates.answer_verification: GeoGebra applet has no key. The brief’s exact (x + 3)^2 + 1 stem is not a catalogue exercise; this is a focused prompt on the selected applet (sliders p, q, a with f(x) = a(x − p)^2 + q).
candidates.reason: Hits the brief’s exact h-sign example. Prediction before the sliders move separates “I read +3 as h = 3” from a later graph check. Fallback: locally bundled JSXGraph; do not require GeoGebra.

candidates.title: Ministry A2.6 sample: vertex of −2(x + 1)^2
candidates.student_facing: Starting from y = x^2, sketch h(x) = −2(x + 1)^2. Where is the vertex? Does this graph have a maximum or a minimum?
candidates.source_stem: Transform the graph of f(x) = x^2 to sketch the graphs of g(x) = x^2 − 4 and h(x) = −2(x + 1)^2.
candidates.answer_verification: Seed has no key for this sample.

provenance.licence: Queen's Printer for Ontario (curriculum excerpt in verified seed)

candidates.reason: Second Ministry plus-inside case. Exposes h-sign on (x + 1) and max-min-from-a (students may use the sign of k, which is 0 here). This is an A2.6 sample reused only for the misconception; do not treat sketching-by-transformation as a new M4 target.

candidates.title: OpenStax worked reading: y = −3(x + 2)^2 + 4
candidates.student_facing: The equation is y = −3(x + 2)^2 + 4. Name the vertex, say whether the graph has a maximum or a minimum, and say how you knew.
candidates.source_stem: Figure 5 represents the graph of the quadratic function written in standard form as y = −3(x + 2)^2 + 4. Since x − h = x + 2 in this example, h = −2. In this form, a = −3, h = −2, and k = 4. Because a < 0, the parabola opens downward. The vertex is at (−2, 4).
candidates.answer: The vertex is at (−2, 4). Because a < 0, the parabola opens downward (vertex is a maximum). h = −2 because x − h = x + 2.
candidates.answer_verification: Copied from OpenStax College Algebra 2e §5.1 worked text on m51274 (Figure 5 paragraph). OpenStax calls a(x − h)^2 + k standard form and also vertex form; Ontario calls that expression vertex form.
instructional_roles: names vertex (h, k) from the equation
candidates.reason: Only selected source that already works the plus-inside reading (x + 2 means h = −2) and ties the sign of a to maximum versus minimum. Use as a semi-worked read-the-equation example, not as a transformation introduction.

candidates.title: MCF3M A2.7 sample: expand 3(x − 1)^2 + 4
candidates.student_facing: Given f(x) = 3(x − 1)^2 + 4, write the same function as ax^2 + bx + c. Use graphing technology to compare the two graphs.
candidates.source_stem: Given the vertex form f(x) = 3(x − 1)^2 + 4, express the equation in standard form. Use technology to compare the graphs of these two forms of the equation.
candidates.answer_verification: Seed has no key for this sample.

provenance.licence: Queen's Printer for Ontario (curriculum excerpt in verified seed)

candidates.reason: Verbatim Ministry sample for A2.7: expand vertex form and check that the graph does not change. Targets the expand-changes-graph misconception. Do not invent the expanded coefficients.

candidates.title: OpenStax: expand ½(x + 2)^2 − 3 and check a table
candidates.student_facing: A graph looks like y = x^2 moved left 2 and down 3, then stretched by one-half: g(x) = (1/2)(x + 2)^2 − 3. Expand this to the ax^2 + bx + c form. Check a few points in a table to see that both writings give the same outputs.
candidates.source_stem: Write an equation for the quadratic function g in Figure 7 as a transformation of f(x) = x^2, and then expand the formula, and simplify terms to write the equation in general form. … In standard form, the algebraic model for this graph is g(x) = (1/2)(x + 2)^2 − 3. To write this in general polynomial form, we can expand the formula and simplify terms. … We can check our work using the table feature on a graphing utility.
candidates.answer_verification: Copied from the OpenStax worked solution on m51274 (Writing the Equation of a Quadratic Function from the Graph). Page typesetting shows the half as 12 in places; the expanded steps give (1/2)x^2 + 2x − 1.
candidates.reason: Second A2.7-shaped worked path: expand, then confirm with a table. Also rehearses h-sign on (x + 2). STAR+diagram if used as a wordless graph-to-equation example; the basketball/shooter follow-on on the same page is A3.3-ish and is not this pick.

candidates.title: OpenStax verbal: advantage of this form
candidates.student_facing: This writing of a quadratic is f(x) = a(x − h)^2 + k. What can you read from it that is harder to see when the same function is written as ax^2 + bx + c?
candidates.source_stem: Explain the advantage of writing a quadratic function in standard form.
candidates.answer: When written in that form, the vertex can be easily identified.
candidates.answer_verification: Copied from OpenStax solution element fs-id1165135361339 (catalogue record openstax-ca2e-m51274-advantage-verbal). OpenStax “standard form” here means a(x − h)^2 + k, which Ontario calls vertex form.
candidates.reason: Verbal A2.10 inspection: what vertex form is for, without asking students to expand. Keep the OpenStax stem in the source field; do not say “standard form” to students without the Ontario naming note.

Graph on the same set of axes f(x) = x^2, f(x) = (x − 2)^2, f(x) = (x − 3)^2, and f(x) = (x + 4)^2.
